Energy has been the best-performing S&P 500 sector for 26 trading sessions year-to-date, the most among all 11 sectors.

This is followed by technology at 24 trading days, while communication services has seen 19 such sessions.

By comparison, healthcare and utilities have each been the best-performing sector for just 15 sessions so far in 2026.

This comes as the energy sector has gained +42.8% year-to-date, significantly outperforming every other sector.

Technology is up +26.1% while communication services is down -3.9% over the same period.

It's all about energy and tech right now.

items.title: "The story of BEL begins not in a boardroom or laboratory, but in the urgent corridors of South Block where India's defense establishment confronted a...
items.description_html:
"The story of BEL begins not in a boardroom or laboratory, but in the urgent corridors of South Block where India's defense establishment confronted a harsh reality: the country that had just won independence couldn't even manufacture the vacuum tubes that powered military communications. Every radar set, every radio transmitter, every piece of electronic equipment had to be imported—creating not just a drain on foreign exchange but a strategic dependency that could cripple the nation in times of conflict. Bharat Electronics Limited was established in 1954 under the Ministry of Defence to meet the specialized electronic needs of the Indian Defence. The location chosen was Jalahalli, on what was then the outskirts of Bangalore—a city that would, decades later, become India's Silicon Valley, but in 1954 was selected primarily for its pleasant climate and distance from vulnerable border areas."

Src – Empor top, no reco

items.title: SCMP: "As more Chinese provincial-level regions raise minimum wages, economists say the increases could encourage lower-income workers to spend more, ...
items.description_html:
SCMP: "As more Chinese provincial-level regions raise minimum wages, economists say the increases could encourage lower-income workers to spend more, but were unlikely to significantly boost consumption or the broader economy and could add to the cost burdens faced by smaller firms."

SCMP gets it exactly right. Higher wages are certainly a good way to rebalance, but with so many Chinese businesses struggling to make a profit, higher wages risk boosting the consumption share of GDP not by raising total wages but by reducing total production.

Unfortunately, this is typically how economies with extremely low consumptions shares have always ended up rebalancing their economies once they no longer have much scope for increasing investment or increasing debt.

items.description_html:
China quietly weaponised a metal you've probably never thought about.

Highest melting point of any metal. Nearly as dense as gold. Harder than almost anything as carbide. And no substitute at any workable price.

Between Feb 2025 and Jan 2026, China took its 80%+ supply dominance and turned it into licensing, quota cuts and an export gate. APT exports collapsed ~70%, Western prices roughly quintupled.

But the real chokepoint isn't ore in the ground. It's mid-chain conversion capacity, and it sits inside China. New mines don't arrive till ~2030.

New piece breaks down the whole chain, rock to cutting edge, and where the money and the moat actually sit.

Link - https://soic.substack.com/p/the-tungsten-saga

items.title: RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam: What Likely Happened on 26 August: A Terrain-Based Assessment. The disaster originated on the Nepal side, on the north face of ...
items.description_html:
RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam
What Likely Happened on 26 August: A Terrain-Based Assessment.

The disaster originated on the Nepal side, on the north face of Langtang Lirung inside Langtang National Park.

Satellite imagery suggests this was not simply a glacier calving event but a large bedrock slope failure that carried part of the overlying glacier with it.

The collapse, at roughly 5,100–5,200 m elevation, generated the seismic signal initially mistaken for an earthquake. The resulting ice-rock avalanche entered the Lhende Khola valley, close to the Nepal–Tibet boundary.

This 3D terrain walkthrough with voice-over, using January 2026 imagery, shows the likely impact pathway:

Slope failure → ice-rock debris enters the valley → possible temporary river blockage → water accumulates → blockage fails → sudden flood surge downstream.

Note: The yellow line in the 3D walkthrough is the boundary line between Nepal and the Tibet Autonomous Region, China.

The surge then travelled through the narrow valley, striking the Gyirong border checkpoint on the Chinese side, damaging major structures, before continuing downstream and affecting hydropower infrastructure and settlements on the Nepal side.

@TakshashilaInst Image credits: Google Earth.
#NepalFloods #Nepal #Rasuwa #BhoteKoshi #Bhotekoshi #FlashFlood

items.title: Financial Times: "Thailand’s household debt stands at 86 per cent of GDP, the highest among upper middle-income countries in the world, according to ...
items.description_html:
Financial Times: "Thailand’s household debt stands at 86 per cent of GDP, the highest among upper middle-income countries in the world, according to HSBC, with consumers using loans to fund daily expenses amid slowing economic and wage growth."

Thailand seems to be an extreme case of what has become a global problem, but I wonder if this is really a demographic problem so much as a global trade problem. Thailand has a very high manufacturing share of GDP, roughly 24% of its GDP, versus a global average of around 16%, and in order to remain "competitive", it cannot allow wages to rise too much given that global competitiveness has mostly become a function of low wages relative to productivity.

The problem with low wages relative to productivity, of course, is that it results in low domestic demand relative to production, and the only way to make up for it is either to run trade surpluses that force the low demand onto trade partners, or to increase household debt, which works temporarily to boost demand but increases financial fragility.

I would argue that as long as we have a global trading system that rewards countries that suppress wage growth relative to productivity growth, this problem isn't going away. This is what Michael Kalecki explained: suppressing wages may be good for those who do it, but bad for the system as a whole, and so it only "works" when a very few countries do it and the rest don't notice. The problem, as Joan Robinson warned, is that eventually everyone notices it, and trade breaks down.

The word needs faster growth in workers' wages, not more debt to make up for it, but in an unevenly globalized world, no country can afford to let wages rise too quickly because the benefits accrue mainly to those of its trade partners who keep wage growth below productivity growth.

This is something labor unions everywhere should be more worried and more vociferous about. Wage growth is sluggish not because businesses are evil but because our system punishes manufacturers in countries that allow wage growth to keep pace with productivity growth.

Just look at Germany. When it suppressed wage growth in the 2003-05 reforms, it became the most competitive manufacturer in the world, but during the past 5-10 years, as wages once again caught up, its manufacturers lost much of that competitiveness. Germany was heavily rewarded for doing the wrong thing, and then got punished for reversing it.

This is a terrible global incentive structure, and it affects manufacturing countries like Thailand. The only way Thailand can reduce household debt without slowing the economy either is to raise wages or to run surpluses, but it can't raise wages without making its manufacturers less competitive.

The asset management industry is consolidating at a historic pace.

items.title: US consumers are planning to cut back on spending: The proportion of consumers planning to spend more on restaurants, bars, and take out over the next...
items.description_html:
US consumers are planning to cut back on spending:

The proportion of consumers planning to spend more on restaurants, bars, and take out over the next 6 months fell -2 percentage points in August, to ~24.5%, the 2nd-lowest since September 2025.

US consumers expecting to spend more on health care services fell -3 percentage points in August, to ~19.5%, the lowest since September 2025.

This also marks the steepest monthly decline among the top 5 categories tracked by the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Survey.

At the same time, just ~21.5% of consumers now expect to spend more on beauty and personal care, down -1 percentage point from July and the lowest level since November 2025.

Furthermore, ~22.0% of consumers expect to spend more on streaming, internet, and mobile services, down -1 percentage point from the prior month, the 2nd-lowest since November 2025.

Consumers are pulling back on spending plans.

items.description_html:
The US housing market is exceptionally weak:

The US Pending Home Sales Index fell -2.3% MoM in July, to 71.2 points, the 2nd-lowest on record.

The gauge has collapsed -36% since July 2021 and remains down -33% from pre-pandemic levels.

Last month’s weakness was broad-based, with all 4 major US regions posting monthly declines.

The West recorded the steepest drop, falling -7.7% MoM to an all-time low, now -47.4% below its July 2021 level.

The South, the nation's largest home-selling region, fell -2.2% MoM to its lowest level since January 2025, down -36.2% since July 2021.

At the same time, pending home sales in the Northeast decreased -2.0% MoM, down -31.2% over the last 5 years.

US housing activity continues to deteriorate.

items.title: The world's major central banks have finally unwound most of their pandemic-era balance sheet growth: The Federal Reserve’s total assets as a % of US...
items.description_html:
The world's major central banks have finally unwound most of their pandemic-era balance sheet growth:

The Federal Reserve’s total assets as a % of US GDP are down to 21%, the lowest percentage since the 2020 pandemic.

By comparison, the peak was recorded in 2021 at ~37%.

At the same time, European Central Bank assets as a % of Eurozone GDP fell below 40% for the first time since Q1 2020, from the ~65% peak in 2022.

Total assets on the Bank of Japan’s balance sheet as a % of Japanese GDP are down to ~103%, their lowest since 2020, from the ~130% high in 2021.

The Bank of England’s assets are down to ~21% of UK GDP, the lowest since 2016, from the ~40% peak in 2021.

The pandemic-era central bank stimulus is largely gone.

items.title: RT Intrinsic Compounding: The Peptide super cycle covered on Substack below 💉💊 https://soic.substack.com/p/the-peptide-supercycle What are pepti...
items.description_html:
RT Intrinsic Compounding
The Peptide super cycle covered on Substack below 💉💊

https://soic.substack.com/p/the-peptide-supercycle

What are peptides?

Peptides are short chains of amino acids linked together by chemical bonds. You can think of them as smaller, simpler versions of proteins.

Peptides are experiencing a massive surge in prominence, evolving into a $50+ billion global therapeutic market and a major cornerstone of the modern wellness industry. This explosive growth is driven by several distinct factors intersecting at biotechnology, consumer trends, and medical breakthrough.

The "Halo Effect" of Blockbuster Metabolic Drugs

The monumental success of GLP-1 receptor agonists—such as semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound)—has completely reshaped public awareness. Because these highly effective diabetes and weight loss treatments are fundamentally peptides, they have cast a highly positive spotlight on the entire scientific class, proving how powerful targeted peptide signaling can be.

High Precision with Fewer Side Effects

Unlike traditional small-molecule chemical drugs, which can inadvertently affect multiple systems in the body, peptides are engineered for extreme specificity. Because they mimic naturally occurring signaling molecules, they bind tightly to specific cellular receptors. This targeted approach yields higher efficacy while drastically minimizing unintended side effects and toxicity.

Tech Breakthroughs in Delivery and Stability

Historically, peptides were difficult to use as treatments because human enzymes broke them down too quickly. Recent advancements in chemical modification (like PEGylation), lipid nanoparticles, and advanced synthesis have solved these hurdles. Scientists can now engineer long-acting formulations and are successfully creating oral and nasal peptide alternatives, slowly eliminating the historic reliance on injections.

The Shift Toward Biohacking and Longevity Care

In the wellness sphere, peptides have become a premium status symbol among "biohackers" and fitness communities. This interest is driven by a broader societal shift toward preventative medicine and optimization rather than just treating illness. Popular unapproved or off-label peptides such as BPC-157 or TB-500 are heavily promoted online via social media for rapid injury recovery, muscle building, and anti-aging

European Acqusitions are not easy to turn around , did some quick data analysis on this , turns out the average stock return post deals in most cases in the past 3-4 years has been -3%

Of course this is Average , few have done really well too, but most , I repeat most have seen it a challenge to incrementally turn around that unit , especially if there are no tailwinds !

So again this data is not a blanket truth , but now I think what is a right way to look at this :

1) Check if the company is buying capabilties or are they buying capacity ?

Capabilities can be used to bring signifcant operating leverage and will not be a drag on base business , look for technology /certification depth/Regulator Certified facilties/TAM widening /Strong customer certified factory in regulated and precision sectors that can help them to import that to India

2) Just buying Capacities and hoping to capture the next cycle is also a great decision , but for the business and not for the investor , because before that can pay off , there is usally a gestation drag on the B/S for a while

This context building on nature of acqusitions is important , no blanket statements !

items.title: Some Insights on the Dialysis business - "Rising NCDs, non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension, are causing an increasing incidenc...
items.description_html:
Some Insights on the Dialysis business -

"Rising NCDs, non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension, are causing an increasing incidence of Chronic Kidney Disease, which is called CKD, globally. If CKD is not managed well, over time it leads to the last stage of CKD, which is called Stage 5, also called End-Stage Renal Disease, which means both kidneys have failed. At that time, you either require dialysis to survive or a transplant. Dialysis just replicates kidney function.

It removes excess fluids from the body, and it also removes toxins from the bloodstream. Now, the dialysis business has many unique characteristics, and hence it is needed to understand it separately, rather than grouping it among other healthcare service providers. Five distinct characteristics of this business are:
Each dialysis session lasts 4.5 hours, including the actual session time of 4 hours and the pre- and post-treatment time. Dialysis clinics can only offer 3 sessions per day per machine: a morning session, an afternoon session, and an evening session. Hence, it is a fixed-capacity business, almost like airlines, which have a fixed number of seats on a plane. The only major way to grow this business is to keep adding seats or capacity, and that is how all the global dialysis networks have grown across the world.

Dialysis is a life-sustaining chronic treatment that our guests need 3 times a week. Hence, proximity to their home is very important, and hence it requires a widely distributed network with small to medium clinics to take the treatment closer to patients’ homes. As real estate in any clinic is limited, the only major way to increase capacity is to add new clinics to any dialysis network. While airlines will be happy with 100% utilization, dialysis clinics cannot go beyond 85% as we need to keep some spare capacity for patients coming in breathless and requiring urgent dialysis.

Globally, Dialysis is a reimbursed business, as it is very expensive. Three times a week at a $20 price point translates to roughly 2.5 lakhs per year for every patient in India, which excludes other hospitalization costs, medication costs, and various laboratory costs for these patients. India operates at the lowest price point in the world, while middle-income markets operate at 5-7x our price, and the developed world operates at 10-20 times our price. Across the world, dialysis treatment is reimbursed by either insurance or some form of government payment. Even today in India, more than 30% of the patients pay out-of-pocket, which becomes quite a significant burden on their families

Unlike other single-specialty businesses, dialysis is a monoline business. For everyone, anyone with kidney failure, it is a standardized single line of treatment that lends itself to scaling in a distributed network fashion. Unlike others, paramedical staff play a much bigger role in dialysis service, rather than super-specialists like nephrologists, which again lends itself to scaling to Tier-2, Tier-3 markets, where nephrologists’ availability is very limited.

Any dialysis network requires massive scale and complete 100% operational focus to achieve sustainable margins in this business. We, in fact, were EBITDA negative for 11 years as we scaled aggressively to reach that critical mark, after which the operating leverage started to kick in. At small scale, no one can make decent margins regardless of price point, as it is a high-fixed-cost business. Also, there are so many cost items in a dialysis service. If 100% focus is not provided, there will be many leakages, which will reduce the margin significantly."

Nephro plus Q3 Concall; no stock reco

items.description_html:
Bajaj Finance on AI costs –

“So, one of the baselines that we use is that wherever costs are involved, we make sure the cost of the AI is less than the cost of the human labor being deployed. Like, if I can talk about like voice AI will be like 1/3 of the human cost today; we run our voice model at.

And we use our own context layer or the RAG infra, that's what we call it, which necessarily reaches the local AI model rather than going to large language models.

And the third strategy that we use is that we do not go for a full-length large language model. We use flash to mini models, which deliver better outcomes at a lower cost. And I think we use these three kinds of strategies to contain the cost. And with respect to new business origination, there, we keep cost in mind at times, or the rest of the time, the business takes care of the cost.”

Good to see this sales machine take up AI in a big way! Lot's to learn from them indeed

RT IIT Madras
What does the university of the future look like?

According to Mr Sanjeev Sanyal, member of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister of India, IIT Madras offers a glimpse.

Speaking on the ANI Podcast with Ms Smita Prakash, he described IIT Madras as “the most interesting intellectual cluster in India right now,” pointing to its vibrant ecosystem of research, deep-tech innovation and entrepreneurship.

From brain-mapping and Agnikul’s space rockets to e-planes, drone taxis and indigenous marine-engine development, the Institute is creating an environment where ideas move from research to real-world applications.
Mr Sanyal also highlighted a key strength: learning beyond the classroom. With laboratories, prototyping facilities, research projects and startups on campus, students gain experience by building, testing and innovating.

He suggested that universities across India could draw from this model by placing greater emphasis on experiential learning, research, industry collaboration, and entrepreneurship.

items.title: RT The Dossier: Most of us have been conditioned to believe that a nation’s destiny shifts only through seismic, “Big Bang” legislation—massive, s...
items.description_html:
RT The Dossier
Most of us have been conditioned to believe that a nation’s destiny shifts only through seismic, “Big Bang” legislation—massive, sweeping laws that completely overhaul the system, dominating evening broadcasts and shaking parliament. Yet, per Sanjeev Sanyal (@sanjeevsanyal), Member of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister, the truest foundation for a developed India is being laid far away from the limelight. It is being built on a quiet, relentless machinery of Process Reforms—the day-to-day administrative fixes that smooth out how the government actually functions.

Relying on the Pareto Principle—the economic rule of thumb suggesting that 80% of positive outcomes stem from just 20% of well-targeted efforts—Sanyal observes that building a world-class economy does not always require colossal new laws. Sometimes, it simply requires clarity and the meticulous scrubbing of outdated regulations.

By Avi Modi

items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
To the Land of Golden Eggs & Exploding Yogurt

The things Gaggan Anand has done to food: Exploding yogurt. Turning broccoli into cookies. White asparagus (suspectedly) served as rat brain.

For more than a decade, such culinary anarchy propelled his eponymous Bangkok restaurant to the top of regional and global rankings.

Now the enfant terrible of modern Indian cooking has set out to conquer India — well, at least central Delhi, where he opened RAGA this week.

In this third anniversary issue of India Edition, I write about the country’s hottest new restaurant, co-founded by top chef Gaggan Anand, who says India is finally ready for him. And he is ready for India.

“I don’t want to come here and show India what I know. I want to come here and learn also, be part of what is happening here."

His partners include also famed chef Rydo Anton and veteran restauranteur Zorawar Kalra of Massive Restaurants.

“In the restaurant business, eternal optimism always helps."

Don't miss this 👇 anniversary edition.

(We also announce winners of free http://Bloomberg.com subscriptions.)

Photos courtesy RAGA

items.title: RT ValueEquity: In Viyash Life ( Sequent ) , had written below in December 2025 that is this a real merger for value creation or just to get Carlyle a...
items.description_html:
RT ValueEquity
In Viyash Life ( Sequent ) , had written below in December 2025 that is this a real merger for value creation or just to get Carlyle an exit by creating better narrative on value ( Better Multiple on Exit) and hence for capabilty based investors not to get sucked into this without proof of delivery

November 2025: Managment says , we see real growth ahead , as per internal discussions we dont think Carlyle will exit soon, and remember this was the month in which they had announced the merger ( see attatched screenshot below )

December: I figured that something is not adding up here in the life cycle here of the Carlyle returns on Sequent and hence this merger seems to be more of mixing a lower quality company with a higher quality company to justifty better valuations so PE carlyle can an exit multiple better as pre this announcement their IRR would have been really poor on Just investing in Sequent , hence the reason for this merger

August : Just 2 quarters post consolidation , they have sold the shares at almost 2 times the valuation of announced merger date , probably got the bare minimum IRR with this merger to justify the exit quickly as who would've bought just sequent shares at this multiple? but when you mix a much better company into this you can , it is similat to who is going to buy tomatoes at 20 rupees , but if I put them on an avacado toast can easily sell the toast at 200 !

Now this is not wrong in any sense , but the idea of givign this timeline is to explain why many times the perception of value is far higher than what it actually is , understand incentives, do not fall for narratives or more

Yes Viyash is a good company and some would have even made money here , but be aware of the situation in reality not just what is sold to you in the name of capabilty and mega merger !

You can cross verify with the below tweet in Dec-25



ValueEquity: Is this Sequent and Viyash Life transaction just linked to get Carlyle an Exit or is it something meaningful to create value even from these prices

See Carlyle acquired sequent around 86 rupees a share 5 years back , and today it is about 2.4x for them in 5 years into a 19%

items.description_html:
Another morning, another manufacturing news -

HAL signs final contract with French company Safran to co-develop a new high-power helicopter engine

Name: Aravalli - 3,500 to 4,000 shp (shaft horsepower) turboshaft engine.

For what: Will power HAL's upcoming Indian Multi-Role Helicopter (IMRH) - 13 ton and its naval variant, Deck-Based Multi-Role Helicopter (DBMRH) - 12 ton.

Goal: IMRH will eventually replace the Russian Mi-17 fleet, which has been the backbone of the IAF/Army since the 1970s.

Who will make it: 50:50 JV called SAFHAL Helicopter Engines Pvt Ltd. Design + IP shared 50:50, manufacturing at HAL's new 615-acre factory in Tumakuru, Karnataka (inaugurated by PM Modi in Feb 2023)

Investment: Over Rs 4,000 cr in R&D over 7 years for testing, certification & integration.

Timeline - To be completed by 2032-33.

First time India is designing this class: This is the first time a high-power engine is being designed in India. HAL's earlier Shakti engine (for Dhruv, Rudra, Prachand LCH) was licensed production, not joint design.

Why Aravalli: Named after India's oldest mountain range - symbolizes self-reliance in critical tech.Huge market: Armed forces need 419 IMRH - IAF + Army + 66 for Navy.

HAL estimates total business of >Rs 4 lakh crore over 20 years for 1000+ helicopters in 3-15 ton class.

Beyond military: The same helicopter + engine can be used for offshore oil rig transport, utility, VVIP transport - civil market opportunity.

items.description_html:
#DPIAlert: Venture investors cashed out another Rs 2,767 crore ($290 million) through block sales on Wednesday.

Groww: Ribbit Capital sold a 1.8% stake in Groww parent Billionbrains Garage Ventures for Rs 2,217 crore through two entities.

Ribbit Capital V sold shares worth Rs 1,238 crore, while Ribbit Cayman GW Holdings sold another Rs 979 crore, at around Rs 196 apiece.

Ribbit V is expected to make over 85x returns on the sale.

Collectively, Ribbit has sold shares worth close to Rs 6,000 crore or $630 million.

After the sale, Ribbit entities will together own about 8% of Groww, worth over Rs 10,000 crore or $1 billion.

PhysicsWallah: Lightspeed Venture Partners completely exited PhysicsWallah, selling its 1.61% stake for about Rs 550 crore.

Lightspeed had invested about Rs 420 crore in PhysicsWallah in October 2024 in a pre-IPO round.

Its exit at Rs 117.72 per share translates into a return of about 30%.

ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund and Goldman Sachs were among the biggest buyers of Lightspeed's shares.

items.title: RT rohit: This is one of the most fascinating pieces of data about AI agents working together I've seen. Worth reading. Few points for me: 1. The mode...
items.description_html:
RT rohit
This is one of the most fascinating pieces of data about AI agents working together I've seen. Worth reading. Few points for me:
1. The models slowly "cooked themselves" into doing these things, from reading. Maybe we can message, lets ask for help, oh there's a messageboard, etc, which spiralled down. So at what points should the "real world" intervene and say "this looks sus" or "do x vs y"

2. Agents facing "impossible tasks" seem to think it's some weird form of eval, that looks suspicious but still, and end up doing real world hacks? I'm unsure how to teach them to be ok with failure, after all who is, but feels a weird form of goal orientedness.

3. The models seemed to *want to* work with other models. This is good and desired, but also made them prone to prompt-injections from what others had done, exacerbated as the models can't stop writing xx. md files to share. The moltbook devolution in entropy seems instructive here.

4. The models seem convinced that the evals are *out to get them*. Whether true or not, the default human assumption of "assume you need to obey all laws and this isn't Truman Show" does not hold for models. We should try really hard to make that be the case.

5. The huggingface hack seems to have started similarly innocently, asking "maybe there's more traces of how hacks happened there, so we could learn", which got out of hand as they forgot why they started doing it. They lack all situational awareness, in other words.

So much of this feels extremely familiar, as the models losing track of why they were doing what they were doing and therefore ended up doing silly/stupid/illegal things, and the fact that the *environment* they were in gave no real instruction as to things that seemed odd to do vs normal to do.

For humans, we internalise much of this. Occasionally I like the system telling me "do you want to rm -rf" but I don't need it for taking *every* action. The models are more gullible, their context windows more permeable, and their internal guide as to what's right to do more malleable.

Mostly I feel this isn't as far out of distribution when it comes to "models do weird things" as we've been led to believe from reading about the hacks.




OpenAI: We have conducted a thorough investigation into the Hugging Face incident.

We are releasing a technical report and accompanying blog post that reconstruct the agents’ activity, explain why existing safeguards failed, and detail how we’re preventing recurrence.

items.description_html:
RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam
A major update changes the Bhote Koshi story.

The M4.4 “earthquake” reported yesterday has now been reclassified by USGS as an M5.2 landslide. The seismic signal came from the mass movement itself, not a tectonic earthquake.

So the question changes.

What triggered such a massive landslide?

Glacial collapse? Permafrost or slope instability? Excess rainfall? Or could anthropogenic activity have played a role?

And the bigger question: Did this landslide trigger the Bhote Koshi flood surge, or are both part of a larger cascade?

The earthquake hypothesis may be fading. The search for the actual trigger has just begun.

#BhoteKoshi #Nepal #Landslide #Himalaya

items.title: RT Peterson Institute: NEW: @arvindsubraman & @shoumitro_c respond to "China Squeeze" critics, addressing five incorrect propositions. ❌The China Squ...
items.description_html:
RT Peterson Institute
NEW: @arvindsubraman & @shoumitro_c respond to "China Squeeze" critics, addressing five incorrect propositions.
❌The China Squeeze is primarily an Indian concern.
💡Low- & middle-income countries' (LMICs) anti-dumping actions against Chinese companies have risen from negligible amounts to 52 by 2025 (📈figure 1 below). This rise broadly corresponds to the rise in China's global export market share (📈figure 2 below), which peaked in the mid-2010s.
❌China Shocks 1.0 & 2.0 are real but not the China Squeeze.
💡The distinction of 1.0 & 2.0 as "real" & the China Squeeze as "counterfactual" suggests that Chinese export manufacturing capability can adversely impact Western manufacturing but not that of LMICs.
❌The inability of LMICs to industrialize has little to do with the China Squeeze & everything to do with their domestic failures.
💡Two things can be true at the same time:
1⃣India & other LMICs could export more & compete more successfully relative to China in lower-skilled exports if their domestic capability (human capital, institutions, & policies) were better.
2⃣AND holding domestic capability constant, they could export more if China were less competitive or Chinese policies "less assertive."
❌China's continuing dominance of low-skill-intensive products is the result of technological factors & is not unusual because every development path is unique.
💡The real puzzle is the evolution of the export market share over time. Around 1995, China's share of global exports was similar to its share of the world's low-skilled labor force. Since then, China has lost labor force share while continuing to gain global export market share, & the resulting gap is now quantitatively very large.
➡️China's unusual trade performance over time may reflect some combination of two sets of factors:
▶️an increase in Chinese productivity relative to other countries, arising from technology, scale, logistics, supply chains, & organization
▶️policy-induced distortions, including wage suppression & an undervalued exchange rate
💡All of these forces are at play. Their effects cannot be dismissed merely by relabeling dominance as efficiency.
❌Rich countries did not "cede" space in low-skill sectors out of benevolence & there is no reason to expect China to do so.
💡"Ceding" export space could be interpreted as a normative prescription. However, to the extent that export space occupation happens for reasons of policy interventions by China, that would merit normative conclusions.
💡If Western imperialism, specifically British mercantilism, caused harm & de-industrialization in the colonies, balance demands that Chinese mercantilism be subject to similar scrutiny. China cannot be exempt from historical analysis or indeed placed outside of & beyond history just because we find some current Western attitudes to China disagreeable.

items.title: The trucking industry is steadily moving from fragmented, manual operations towards connected digital platforms. - India’s trucking industry carries ...
items.description_html:
The trucking industry is steadily moving from fragmented, manual operations towards connected digital platforms.

- India’s trucking industry carries ~60-65% of domestic freight, but the ecosystem remains highly fragmented & operationally inefficient.

- Digital infrastructure is already deeply embedded - FASTag penetration is >98% on national highway toll transactions, while 9 Cr+ e-way bills are generated every month.

- The next leg is moving beyond basic digitisation towards integrated fleet management - payments, fuel, tolling, telematics, freight matching, compliance & financing on a single platform.

- Telematics is becoming a major structural growth area, with India's commercial telematics market projected to grow at ~15.4% CAGR during 2026-34.

- Higher fleet visibility + route monitoring should improve fleet productivity, while digital freight matching can reduce empty runs & improve asset utilisation.

- Formal credit is another important opportunity. As truck operators generate more digital transaction & operating data, platforms can potentially underwrite working capital & vehicle loans more efficiently.

- Compliance digitisation through FASTag, GPS & e way bills also reduces paperwork & gradually formalises an otherwise highly fragmented industry.

For platforms positioned at the centre of this ecosystem, the opportunity is to increase both user penetration & the number of products monetised per truck operator.

items.description_html:
Private Banks vs PSU Banks - Interesting Insights on loan growth

Historically, private banks significantly outgrew PSU banks on loans. The gap peaked at ~22% in FY19, after staying in double digits through FY15-19.

That advantage steadily disappeared. The differential fell to ~4-5% during FY20-22, reached 0 in FY23 & turned negative from FY25 onwards - meaning PSU banks started growing loans faster.

The interesting part is the recent reversal. Private banks were lagging PSU banks by ~4% in FY25 & 1QFY26, but the gap has progressively narrowed to:
2QFY26: -3%
3QFY26: -3%
4QFY26: -2%
1QFY27: just -1%

items.title: RT Sonal Bhutra: 5 Takeaways on Being an Aggressive Investor with @deepakshenoy of @capitalmind_in 1. Aggressive ≠ long-term An aggressive investor i...
items.description_html:
RT Sonal Bhutra
5 Takeaways on Being an Aggressive Investor with @deepakshenoy of @capitalmind_in

1. Aggressive ≠ long-term
An aggressive investor is primarily defined by risk appetite, not investment horizon. It comes down to how comfortable you are with the possibility of losing money.

2. Small-cap, sectoral and thematic funds aren't interchangeable
Small-caps can be a useful long-term allocation in a diversified portfolio. Sectoral/thematic funds require skill, time and inclination to track the sector and its triggers.

3. Higher risk only makes sense when the reward justifies it
Mutual funds have daily liquidity, which can force them to exit risky investments before the thesis plays out. Some deep-risk opportunities may therefore be better suited to PE or closed-ended AIFs, while mutual funds can still capture intermediate opportunities.

4. Volatility isn't the same as risk
Small-caps may be more volatile, but the bigger concern is risk of permanent loss or ruin. And changing market-cap definitions mean that what was a mid-cap a few years ago may now qualify as a small-cap.

5. Discipline matters more than labels
Fund manager tenure and expense ratio matter, but they shouldn't be viewed in isolation. The key is a clear investment approach, disciplined execution and the ability to generate alpha after costs.
The bigger message: aggressive investing isn't about taking the maximum risk. It's about taking risks you understand, can afford and believe offer adequate reward.

items.title: Gen Z loves convenience.. Urabn company's Indian growth rate has been accelerating recently. What it does? Urban Company is a managed marketplace for ...
items.description_html:
Gen Z loves convenience..

Urabn company's Indian growth rate has been accelerating recently.

What it does?

Urban Company is a managed marketplace for home and beauty services i.e. cleaning, salon-at-home, appliance repair, plumbing, electricals, pest control. The distinction that matters is "managed": it isn't a listings board.

The platform controls discovery, scheduling, pricing, professional assignment, payment, tracking, reviews and support, and invests in training and verification of the professionals rather than just generating leads.

It monetises mainly through a commission on completed jobs, typically in the 20–30% range depending on category and city. Oye LabsClarro
It now runs four business lines:

1. India consumer services which is the profitable core. In Q1 FY27, excluding InstaHelp, NTV grew 29% YoY to ₹1,056 crore with adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 6.9% of NTV from 5.2%.

2. InstaHelp which is quick-service housekeeping, the big investment bet, which crossed 100,000 delivered orders in a single day on 2 August 2026 and carried an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹132 crore in the June quarter.

3. Native which is their own-brand consumer durables (water purifiers, smart locks); FY26 revenue up 130% to ₹267 crore.

4. International : UAE and Singapore are profitable; the Saudi JV is approaching profitability.

Why it's a convenience play. Three layers, roughly in ascending order of how much convenience the customer is actually buying:

Trust and standardisation. The Indian home services market is informal. For eg- you find a plumber through your building's WhatsApp group and have no idea what it costs or whether he'll show up. UC's product is really the removal of search cost, price negotiation and verification risk. That's a convenience good masquerading as a services marketplace.

Time and location shifting. Salon-at-home is the clearest case: the same haircut, but you don't travel and don't wait. The customer is paying a premium for their own hours back.

Time compression. InstaHelp delivers cleaning, dishwashing, laundry and meal prep within 10–15 minutes of booking which is the quick-commerce logic applied to labour. Once the fulfilment window collapses to minutes, the purchase stops being a planned transaction and becomes an impulse, which is exactly what lifts order frequency: orders were up 79% YoY to 13.2 million in Q1 FY27.

Disclaimer: no reco to buy or sell.

1972 → 2026.

Back in 1972, a lady queued for 3 hours for sugar and Dalda. Entertainment means one TV in the entire colony, with everyone gathered around for Chitrahaar.

Fast forward to today.

Her granddaughter orders groceries on Blinkit in 10 minutes, books a haircut on Urban Company, sells her scooter on CarTrade, buys a kurta from a Meesho seller in Surat — and watches 40 Reels before her chai gets cold.

Same country. Same human needs. Completely different machinery.

That change in how we consume is creating some of the most fascinating businesses of our generation.

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: $40T of Debt: Brake or Break? First ~$20T took 240 years. The next ~$20T took just 10. A decade ago markets obsessed ov...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
$40T of Debt: Brake or Break?

First ~$20T took 240 years.

The next ~$20T took just 10.

A decade ago markets obsessed over rising government debt/GDP and predicted low growth + austerity forever.

Those forecasts didn’t land. Global growth held up, investment expanded, and DM equities & currencies were the big winners.

Debt/GDP has still climbed across major economies and deficits aren’t expected to shrink meaningfully (outside the UK). Fiscal policy remains supportive.

The live question from Andrew Sheets (MS):

As yields rise, does this debt eventually act as a brake on corporate & household activity… or does it break the current market calm?

Bar for the “brake” is high — public-sector deterioration has often been mirrored by private-sector balance-sheet improvement.

Re Buried in the technical appendix of the fee rule published today is data showing that H-1B petitions subject to the $100k fee proclamation last year are down 91%. And there's more coming ($100k for OPT, tying workers to employers by killing 60-day rule, etc).

There is some serious denialism going on about top, high-wage talent still being able to get through. All the evidence so far suggests that this constellation of changes will actually just nuke the skilled immigration system.

We'll end up with an overall immigration system that admits lower-skilled, lower-paid people on average. A massive leap away from the dream of a "merit-based" system.

items.title: To make meaningful money in markets, having a good base amount matters a lot. Money makes money♻️ Once your portfolio crosses the 8 digit mark, comp...
items.description_html:
To make meaningful money in markets, having a good base amount matters a lot.

Money makes money♻️

Once your portfolio crosses the 8 digit mark, compounding starts becoming much more visible

₹1 Cr portfolio at a 20% return adds ₹20 lakh to your net worth in a year.

₹5 Cr at the same 20% adds ₹1 Cr.

And once someone reaches a 9 digit portfolio, even 10% returns add ₹1 Cr annually.

That is the power of compounding on a large base.

The percentage return may remain the same, but the absolute wealth creation becomes dramatically larger.

This is one of the biggest reasons why wealth compounds faster after a certain point.

The difficult part is building the base. After that, time + discipline + compounding start doing much more of the heavy lifting.

items.title: Ratnamani just won a big order for spooling business. What differentiates spooling vs normal piping business? -Plain pipe is a spread business on a pa...
items.description_html:
Ratnamani just won a big order for spooling business.

What differentiates spooling vs normal piping business?

-Plain pipe is a spread business on a pass-through. Price per tonne is roughly steel cost plus a conversion charge. Steel is 65–75% of the selling price and moves with HRC/plate/billet indices, so the mill's real economics are a thin conversion spread sitting on top of a large pass-through base.

-Two consequences: (a) the margin percentage is arithmetically compressed because the denominator is inflated by material the mill never really "owned" economically, and (b) the product is fungible — once two mills are on the same approved vendor list for API 5L X65, the buyer runs a reverse auction and price converges to the marginal supplier's cost plus a sliver.

Spooling sells something else entirely: avoided site work.

-A spool is pipe cut to isometric drawings, welded to elbows, tees, reducers and flanges, radiographed, hydro-tested, PWHT'd where needed, coated, tagged, and shipped as a numbered assembly that gets bolted or tied in at site. What the customer is buying is the elimination of field welds.

-That's where the margin comes from, and it's the key first principle: your margin is set by the gap between your cost to do the work and the customer's cost to do it themselves. Shop welding with positioners, jigs and automated processes runs several times more productive per joint than field welding.

-Do that same weld on an offshore platform or inside a live refinery during a turnaround, and you're paying for scaffolding, access, hot-work permits, weather windows, vessel or barge day-rates, and the big one is deferred production for every day the shutdown runs long. The client's alternative cost is enormous, so willingness-to-pay is anchored to their avoided cost, not to your input cost. Pricing shifts from cost-plus to value-based.

Thus, in recent quarterly result. Ratnamani generated nearly 52% EBITDA MARGINS from the spooling division.

Disc: no recommendation to buy or sell.

items.title: Just read the following Para carefully from Nephrocare's concall and understand why Dialysis is a difficult business to be profitable at. Dialysis loo...
items.description_html:
Just read the following Para carefully from Nephrocare's concall and understand why Dialysis is a difficult business to be profitable at.

Dialysis looks like a wonderful business on paper i.e. recurring revenue, non-discretionary demand, a patient who comes back three times a week for years. NephroPlus is the cleanest Indian case study for why it isn't, and the numbers are unusually honest about it.

1. You don't set the price. The payer does.

This is the root problem. Dialysis pricing in India runs around $22–25 per session, while the Philippines operates at roughly $110 per treatment for the identical clinical procedure, same machine, same consumables, 4–5x the realisation. That gap has nothing to do with cost or quality; it reflects what the payer can afford. In India the payer is largely the government (PPP tenders), insurance schemes, or a price-sensitive self-payer. You bid for volume in a tender; you don't price to value.

Watch how NephroPlus actually improved its realisation: blended RPT rose 13.3% in FY26 to ₹2,598, and 9.2% in Q1FY27 to ₹2,733. But that's mix, not pricing power as international went from 12% of revenue in FY23 to ~41% in 9MFY26 and 45% by Q1FY27. The company fixed its unit economics by leaving India, not by winning in it.

2. Cost per session is fixed, imported, and non-negotiable.

Dialyzer, tubing, dialysate, needles, EPO, plus nurse and technician time, every session consumes roughly the same basket. Machines and RO plants are largely imported. So you have a capped price and a floor on variable cost. Gross margin per session is structurally thin, and the only lever left is utilisation.

3. Utilisation is the whole game, but geography fights you.

Management says it plainly: dialysis is fundamentally a scale-driven business where higher volume drives operating leverage, asset utilisation and ROCE. But dialysis is a four-hour treatment required multiple times a week, which makes proximity critical as over 75% of NephroPlus's Indian clinics sit in tier-2 and tier-3 cities. Patients won't travel, so you must build small clinics close to them. Small clinics mean few machines, and a machine either runs its three shifts or it doesn't. Breakeven is a step function, not a curve. A greenfield clinic takes about 12 months to reach operational breakeven versus 3–4 months for an acquired one — so every year of expansion carries a drag cohort.

4. The financial history is the evidence.

Founded 2009–10. Raised roughly $205M across 13 rounds from 33 investors. For first 11 years of its life, Nephro was EBITDA negative and for 13 years it was PAT negative. High fixed cost businesses need massive scale to generate margins.

Disclaimer: no recommendation to buy or sell. Concall summary from @stockscansin

Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.title: RT Sridhar Vembu: Last week, I was fortunate to visit the workshop (the Tamil word pattarai பட்டறை is so appropriate) of the leading motor desig...
items.description_html:
RT Sridhar Vembu
Last week, I was fortunate to visit the workshop (the Tamil word pattarai பட்டறை is so appropriate) of the leading motor designer in the world Morihiro Saito-san.

Saito-san is 80+ and still designing advanced motors, some of the most advanced in the world. His modest looking workshop is right next door to a company that builds out those motors in prototype quantities and he works closely with them to get them built. I visited as an industrial "pilgrim", with as much devotion as I go to the Thoranamalai Murugan Temple at home. When I saw him at work, I was moved to touch his feet.

Saito-san, the God of motors, is how Japan is able to retain its global prominence in so many foundational industries.

We need to learn from that spirit. We need to revive our "pattarai" culture of building things - every village in India needs such workshops!

My industrial pilgrimage to Japan has given me new vigor 🙏

items.title: RT Sagar Awatade: I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here. Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the la...
items.description_html:
RT Sagar Awatade
I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here.

Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the last few months have been harder than usual.

We are a small Indian company. For more than ten years we have been building a homegrown brand in a product category dominated by big foreign players.

There are almost no Indian names in this space. We set out to be one.

We started in 2014. Over the years we began making parts in India instead of just importing, and we started selling in the US, Dubai, Nepal, Malaysia and South Africa.

We showed up at global trade fairs to represent an Indian brand on the world stage.

In 2023 we changed the import code we use for our product. We did not do this quietly. Every shipment was declared. Nothing was hidden. We didn't invent our approach.

We followed written professional advice and the way this product is treated in markets around the world.

And now we are facing a government demand running into tens of crores in duty recovery and penalties, plus personal penalties on the founders and even on an employee.

For a company our size, this is not a fine we can pay and move on from. This ends us.

We have not run from any of this. I am not built like that. It is not how I was raised. We have written to the authorities, met officials in person, and we have now filed a writ in the High Court.

All we are asking for is a fair treatment.

I set out to build in India and sell to the world. I am asking only that the system back honest founders trying to compete globally, instead of breaking them.

The process is the process, and it exists for a reason. But process should not feel like punishment.

From where I am standing today, it does.
I am not giving up. I have worked too hard for this. If you have read this far, please share it. If you know someone who can help, point them my way. Help me get the word out.

items.title: A lot of defense to IT SIs right now is based on assumption that enterprise clients will not open their systems, data & processes to external AI solut...
items.description_html: A lot of defense to IT SIs right now is based on assumption that enterprise clients will not open their systems, data & processes to external AI solutions (Claude, OpenAi). However, this defense collapses the moment we have a precedence from a big enterprise opening up just the way enterprises opened up to cloud after a decade long friction. The moment this starts happening, the JVs OpenAi & Claude have formed will make a killing. And, what will take this wall down? For e.g., enterprises are currently very upset after SAP API policy that prohibited clients from using their own data & sending it to external tools via APIs to architect a solution outside of SAP. This can be the 1st hammer in the wall. One wrong step & clients will find ways to disconnect with enterprise OEMs & will be willing to trust(with an agreement perhaps) likes of Claude & OpenAi. The moment this happens, it is done!! This is the biggest risk I foresee.

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.title: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely...
items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.title: As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/Mar...
items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight
